blocks.content: Availability means your system is up and reachable the moment a user actually tries to use it. Not just technically running somewhere, genuinely serving requests correctly, right now, for this user.

This topic covers exactly how availability is measured, the single mental model that explains almost every availability decision in system design, how and why real systems actually fail, and the concrete patterns, redundancy, failover, geographic distribution, and circuit breaking, that turn a fragile system into a highly available one.
1. What Is Availability

Think of availability like a hospital emergency room. It does not matter how skilled the doctors are if the ER is closed the moment you arrive, it is useless to you right then. High availability means the ER stays open around the clock, even when individual doctors are out sick, equipment fails, or the power flickers.

blocks.title: Availability Is Not Reliability
blocks.content: A vending machine that is always on but occasionally gives the wrong snack is highly available but unreliable. A vending machine that works perfectly when it is running but shuts down at random is reliable but not available. Both properties matter, and they solve genuinely different problems.
In system design, we design for availability by assuming components will fail, not by hoping they will not, and making sure the system keeps working anyway.
2. Measuring Availability: The Nines

Availability is measured as the percentage of time a system is operational over a period, usually a year. A system that was up for 364 of 365 days sits at roughly 99.73 percent, just below what the industry calls three nines.

Each additional nine of availability shrinks the allowed downtime dramatically, roughly by a factor of ten each time, which is exactly why the jump from three nines to five nines is so much harder and more expensive to achieve than it sounds.

{"headers":["Availability","Allowed Downtime Per Year","Typical Use Case"],"rows":[["99 percent, two nines","About 3.65 days","Small applications, personal projects"],["99.9 percent, three nines","About 8.76 hours","Common for modern web applications and SaaS products"],["99.99 percent, four nines","About 52 minutes","Banking systems, cloud platforms, enterprise services"],["99.999 percent, five nines","About 5 minutes","Payment systems, telecom networks"],["99.9999 percent, six nines","A few seconds","Mission critical infrastructure, aerospace, military systems"]]}
As the number of nines increases, the system becomes more reliable, but the engineering complexity and cost increase just as sharply.

The right target is never about maximizing nines for its own sake, it is about the actual business cost of downtime. Most payment systems reasonably target four nines. An internal admin dashboard is usually fine at three nines. A handful of businesses like Netflix and AWS aim for five nines or beyond, because for them, an hour of downtime is genuinely catastrophic.
3. Series vs Parallel: The Core Mental Model
blocks.text: 3. Series vs Parallel: The Core Mental Model

blocks.content: This is one of the most important mental models in all of high level design. How you connect components completely changes a system's overall availability, in a direction that surprises most people the first time they see the math.
Components in Series
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396519049-621466435.png
blocks.alt: To catch a flight, every single step, check in, security, boarding, must succeed, one failure anywhere ends the whole journey

blocks.content: When every component in a chain must work for the overall system to work, their availabilities multiply together, and the result always goes down. If check in, security, and boarding are each 99.9 percent reliable individually, the odds all three succeed together are 0.999 multiplied three times, roughly 99.7 percent, worse than any single step on its own.

blocks.title: Ask This In Every Design Interview
blocks.content: What is the critical path here, and exactly how many dependencies must all succeed for one request to succeed? Every extra step on that critical path is additional risk, even if each individual step is highly reliable.
Components in Parallel
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785270960200-897037885.png
blocks.alt: A supermarket with several open checkout lanes needs every single one to close before a customer goes unserved

blocks.content: When any one of several components can independently handle a request, availability compounds dramatically in your favor instead. If two servers are each independently down only 0.1 percent of the time, the odds both are down at the exact same moment are 0.1 percent multiplied by 0.1 percent, just 0.0001 percent, meaning the pair is available 99.9999 percent of the time, six nines, built from two ordinary three nine components.
Parallel components are the entire reason high availability is achievable at all.
4. Why Systems Actually Fail
Before designing for availability, you need a clear picture of how things actually fail. Most real outages combine more than one of these categories at once.
Hardware Failures

Physical components wear out, and at scale this is routine, not exceptional. A data center running ten thousand servers sees hundreds of hardware failures every year. A system built for real availability treats this as a daily occurrence to design around, not a rare emergency to react to.
Software Failures

These are trickier than hardware failures because they depend on input, state, and timing rather than physical wear, a bug can sit dormant through months of testing and only fire under one specific production condition.

["Bugs are coding mistakes that only cause crashes or wrong output under certain conditions, which is exactly what makes them hard to find in advance","Memory leaks grow steadily over time until the system slows down or crashes outright, a slow death rather than a sudden one","Deadlocks happen when two or more processes wait on each other forever, freezing the system in place","Cascading failures start as one service failing and end as a domino effect across every service that depends on it"]
items: Bugs are coding mistakes that only cause crashes or wrong output under certain conditions, which is exactly what makes them hard to find in advance
Memory leaks grow steadily over time until the system slows down or crashes outright, a slow death rather than a sudden one
Deadlocks happen when two or more processes wait on each other forever, freezing the system in place
Cascading failures start as one service failing and end as a domino effect across every service that depends on it

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396519049-25304358.png
blocks.alt: Service B slows down, Service A's threads pile up waiting on it, and Service C, which depends on A, fails too, even though the original problem was B's database

blocks.title: A Real Cascading Failure
blocks.content: Service A calls Service B. Service B slows down because its own database is overloaded. Service A's threads pile up waiting for B to respond, until A itself runs out of threads. Now Service C, which calls A, fails too. The original problem was B's database, but the visible failure is the entire platform.
Network Failures
Network failures tend to be intermittent and hard to reproduce, which makes them more frustrating to debug than a clean hardware crash.

["Packet loss means data fails to reach its destination, causing requests to time out with no clear error at all","Latency spikes cause sudden delays that trigger timeouts even though the network itself is technically still working","A network partition splits servers into groups that each believe the others are down, the classic split brain problem","A DNS failure stops the system that converts service names into addresses, so services can no longer find each other"]
items: Packet loss means data fails to reach its destination, causing requests to time out with no clear error at all
Latency spikes cause sudden delays that trigger timeouts even though the network itself is technically still working
A network partition splits servers into groups that each believe the others are down, the classic split brain problem
A DNS failure stops the system that converts service names into addresses, so services can no longer find each other

blocks.content: Human Error
A large share of real world outages trace back to people, not hardware or software: a wrong environment variable, a bad migration, a destructive command run in production instead of staging.

blocks.title: Why Automation Matters So Much
blocks.content: This is exactly why mature teams invest heavily in CI CD pipelines, automated rollbacks, configuration validation, and staging environments. The goal is not to blame people, it is to design systems where common mistakes are either prevented at the source or quickly reversible.
5. Redundancy: The Foundation of Availability
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396519050-349881620.png
blocks.alt: Real availability means every layer, DNS, load balancers, application servers, and the database, has its own redundancy, not just one

blocks.content: Every availability strategy eventually comes back to one idea: have more than one of the thing that can fail. If one copy fails, another takes over. Simple in concept, genuinely deep in execution.

Redundancy is never free, every backup server, every replica, every extra availability zone costs real money. The question worth asking is always whether the cost of that redundancy is smaller than the cost of the downtime it actually prevents.

blocks.title: The Weakest Link Rule
blocks.content: Redundancy at one layer means nothing if the layer beneath it is a single point of failure. Ten redundant application servers are useless if all ten depend on one single database. Redundancy has to exist at every critical layer, not just the one that happened to get attention first.
6. Active Passive vs Active Active
Once you decide to run redundant components, you still need to decide how they actually work together. There are two dominant approaches, and they trade cost for speed differently.
Active Passive
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785270965334-978565657.png
blocks.alt: One node does all the real work while a standby sits idle, ready to take over the moment the primary fails

blocks.content: One node handles all the traffic. A second node sits idle, ready to take over if the first one fails. That handoff is called a failover. A car's spare tire does zero work while you are driving, the moment you get a flat, you swap it in, it does not make the car faster, it only saves you when something goes wrong. That is active passive.

If the network link between primary and standby breaks, both can sometimes promote themselves to primary at once, and data quietly diverges. This is the split brain problem, solved with a quorum requiring several nodes to agree, a fencing mechanism, or an external arbitrator.
Active Active
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785270967025-61018166.png
blocks.alt: Every node already serves real traffic, so a failure is handled by simply no longer routing to it, with no failover step at all

blocks.content: All nodes serve real traffic simultaneously. When one fails, the load balancer simply stops routing to it, there is no failover step, because the other nodes were already doing real work the whole time. A supermarket with six open checkout lanes does not need to activate a new lane when one breaks, the other five simply absorb the extra customers immediately.

Active active works naturally for stateless services, where any server can handle any request. Stateful services need either shared storage or sticky sessions to make it work, and sticky sessions quietly reduce the availability benefit, since a user is once again tied to one specific node.
7. Geographic Redundancy
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785270968632-727720059.png
blocks.alt: Traffic is spread across separate geographic regions, so an outage in one region does not take the whole system down

blocks.content: Redundancy inside a single data center protects you against hardware failure. It does nothing if the entire building loses power, a fiber line is cut, or a natural disaster hits the region. That is what geographic redundancy solves, spreading a system across physically separate locations entirely.

A single bank branch burning down means you cannot access your account there. A bank with a hundred branches across the country means you simply walk to the next one. A multi availability zone deployment is like branches in the same city, close enough for fast, synchronous replication. A multi region deployment is like branches in different states, far enough apart to survive a regional disaster, at the cost of fifty to one hundred fifty milliseconds of added latency on every synchronous write.
Most multi region systems accept asynchronous replication instead, and accept that in a genuine disaster, the last few seconds of writes might be lost.

blocks.title: RPO and RTO
blocks.content: Multi region replication forces you to define two numbers explicitly. Recovery Point Objective is how much data loss is acceptable in a disaster. Recovery Time Objective is how long the system is allowed to stay down before it recovers. Both are business decisions first, technical decisions second.
8. High Availability Patterns in Practice
Four patterns show up in almost every genuinely highly available system, and each one solves one specific failure mode from earlier in this topic.
Load Balancer with Health Checks

A load balancer continuously pings every backend server. One that fails its health check is pulled from rotation within seconds, and traffic shifts to the healthy servers automatically, while a new server can join the pool without any downtime at all. An air traffic control tower constantly monitors every runway, if one is blocked, planes are routed to another instantly, passengers never even notice. Note that the load balancer itself becomes a new single point of failure unless it is made redundant too, exactly the weakest link rule from earlier.
Database Replication with Automatic Failover

Databases hold real state, so you cannot simply load balance across them the way you do with stateless web servers. A primary handles reads and writes while one or more replicas stay synced, and if the primary fails, a replica is automatically promoted to take its place.

A common production setup uses synchronous replication to the one replica designated for failover, guaranteeing zero data loss, and asynchronous replication to every other read replica and analytics system, avoiding any added latency on the write path. Best of both approaches, applied where each one actually matters.
Queue Based Load Leveling
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785270970446-152517029.png
blocks.alt: A sudden traffic spike fills the queue instead of overwhelming the database, letting workers drain it at a pace the system can sustain

blocks.content: A message queue sits between producers and consumers. When traffic spikes, requests fill the queue instead of overwhelming the database, and workers consume at a sustainable rate. If a worker crashes mid task, the message simply waits in the queue rather than disappearing. Restaurant orders go onto printed tickets, if a cook goes home sick, the tickets wait on the rail rather than vanishing, and a sudden dinner rush fills the ticket rail, not the kitchen itself. Without a queue, a flash sale generating a hundred times normal traffic for five minutes would crush the database outright.
Circuit Breaker
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396519051-515563114.png
blocks.alt: A circuit breaker moves between closed, open, and half open, stopping calls to a failing dependency before it drags everything else down with it

blocks.content: When a dependency starts failing, continuing to call it wastes threads and risks the exact cascading failure covered earlier in this topic. A circuit breaker watches the failure rate, and once it crosses a set threshold, it opens, every call immediately returns an error without even attempting the dependency. After a timeout, it lets exactly one test request through to check whether the dependency has recovered.

An electrical circuit breaker at home trips the instant a short circuit happens, cutting power to that one zone to protect the rest of the house, rather than leaving current flowing into a broken wire. A software circuit breaker does exactly the same thing, cutting the call to a broken service before it drags everything else down with it. This exact pattern, the circuit breaker's closed, open, and half open states, is covered in full depth in the API Gateway problem elsewhere on this platform.
9. A Common Mistake: Redundancy at the Wrong Layer
blocks.text: 9. A Common Mistake: Redundancy at the Wrong Layer

blocks.content: A suspension bridge has hundreds of redundant cables, but if the single anchor point holding one end of the bridge fails, every one of those cables fails together. Redundancy at the wrong layer solves nothing at all.

This exact mistake shows up constantly in real systems: a team builds ten redundant application servers, feels confident about availability, and never notices that all ten depend on one single database with no replica and no failover path. The visible layer got redundancy, the layer that actually mattered did not.

blocks.title: Ask This Before Declaring a System Highly Available
blocks.content: For every layer in the request path, DNS, load balancer, application server, cache, database, ask specifically what happens if this exact layer fails right now. A system is only as available as its least redundant layer, never its most redundant one.
Key Takeaway

Availability is the percentage of time a system is genuinely up and reachable, measured in nines, where each additional nine cuts allowable downtime by roughly a factor of ten. Components in series multiply availability down, components in parallel compound it up, and that single insight drives most high level design decisions around redundancy. Real systems fail from hardware wear, software bugs, network issues, and human error in routine, predictable ways, and the fix is always the same underlying idea: have more than one of the thing that can fail, at every layer that actually matters, not just the one that is easiest to make redundant.
